frictionVectors.title: European gas dependence
frictionVectors.details: Algeria retains strong control over hydrocarbons and uses pipeline and LNG exports to preserve bargaining power with Europe. EU pressure for supply diversification and lower-carbon energy could gradually weaken this leverage.

frictionVectors.title: Sahel security spillover
frictionVectors.details: Instability across Mali, Niger, and Libya places pressure on Algeria's borders and complicates energy infrastructure protection. Algiers is resisting deeper foreign military involvement while balancing regional mediation.

frictionVectors.title: Hydrocarbon concentration
frictionVectors.details: Angola controls its petroleum sector formally, but fiscal stability remains highly exposed to oil prices, declining mature fields, and foreign technical capital. Production-sharing arrangements limit the state's effective capture of value.

frictionVectors.title: Debt-linked infrastructure
frictionVectors.details: Chinese-financed rail, power, and construction projects remain strategically important and contribute to external financing dependence. Luanda is diversifying toward Gulf, Western, and domestic investors to reduce concentration risk.

frictionVectors.title: Niger and Burkina border insecurity
frictionVectors.details: Jihadist violence in northern Benin threatens transport corridors, agricultural zones, and state access to frontier communities. Security cooperation with regional and Western partners is expanding but also increases reliance on external support.

frictionVectors.title: Regional trade dependence
frictionVectors.details: The Port of Cotonou is central to Benin's economic sovereignty but remains sensitive to Nigerian border policy and wider coastal trade disruptions. Port modernization and logistics reforms are improving national leverage while attracting foreign commercial influence.

frictionVectors.title: Diamond market concentration
frictionVectors.details: Botswana retains substantial negotiating power through its partnership with De Beers, but public revenues and foreign exchange remain exposed to global diamond demand. Efforts to expand domestic cutting, beneficiation, and alternative minerals are strategically important.

frictionVectors.title: Critical-minerals competition
frictionVectors.details: Foreign interest in copper, nickel, lithium, and other minerals could accelerate development but create pressure over licensing terms and local value addition. Botswana's institutions provide stronger safeguards than many regional peers.

frictionVectors.title: Russian security dependence
frictionVectors.details: Ouagadougou is reducing reliance on France and deepening security ties with Russia and other non-Western partners. This increases room for maneuver but raises concerns over opaque contracts, accountability, and possible concessions linked to security assistance.

frictionVectors.title: Mining-sector disruption
frictionVectors.details: Gold remains the backbone of export earnings, yet insurgent attacks and state control gaps threaten mines, roads, and artisanal production. The government's effort to tighten national control over mining is constrained by insecurity and limited processing capacity.

frictionVectors.title: Critical Minerals Dependence
frictionVectors.details: Burundi is seeking foreign capital and technical partners to develop nickel and other mineral deposits, limiting its near-term control over value chains. Export infrastructure and opaque licensing remain major sovereignty risks.

frictionVectors.title: Regional Security Rivalry
frictionVectors.details: Relations with Rwanda remain strained over armed groups and cross-border accusations, while eastern DRC instability complicates trade and security planning. Burundi’s dependence on regional corridors increases its exposure.

frictionVectors.title: External Infrastructure Finance
frictionVectors.details: Ports, airports, digital networks, and maritime-security projects rely heavily on European, Chinese, and multilateral financing. The government retains strong institutional oversight but must manage debt and strategic access concerns.

frictionVectors.title: Tourism and Energy Exposure
frictionVectors.details: The economy remains vulnerable to external tourism cycles, imported fuel costs, and climate stress. Renewable-energy expansion could improve sovereignty, but financing and grid capacity remain constraints.

highlights: Oil, Gas, and Timber Under Pressure

frictionVectors.title: Foreign-Controlled Resource Chains
frictionVectors.details: Hydrocarbon, mining, timber, and major infrastructure projects depend substantially on foreign firms and lenders. Weak transparency and limited domestic processing reduce Cameroon’s control over resource rents.

frictionVectors.title: Anglophone Conflict and Corridors
frictionVectors.details: Fighting in the Northwest and Southwest continues to disrupt transport, public authority, and investment confidence. Instability also threatens strategic routes linking the interior to Atlantic ports.

frictionVectors.title: Russian Security and Mining Access
frictionVectors.details: The government relies on Russian-linked security personnel and political support, while foreign actors seek influence over gold and diamond production. Weak oversight risks converting security dependence into long-term concessions.

frictionVectors.title: Corridor Dependence
frictionVectors.details: Landlocked trade depends heavily on routes through Cameroon and neighboring states, leaving fuel, food, and mineral exports vulnerable to insecurity and border disruptions. Limited state presence outside Bangui further constrains infrastructure sovereignty.

frictionVectors.title: Oil and Pipeline Dependence
frictionVectors.details: Chad’s fiscal model remains centered on oil exports through the Cameroon pipeline, giving foreign operators and transit infrastructure significant leverage. Price volatility and limited domestic refining weaken sovereign control.

frictionVectors.title: External Security Balancing
frictionVectors.details: The government is recalibrating ties after France’s military drawdown while managing threats from Sudan, Libya, and Sahel insurgencies. Gulf, Russian, and regional actors may gain influence as N'Djamena diversifies security partnerships.

frictionVectors.title: French control of Mayotte
frictionVectors.details: France retains control of Mayotte, sustaining a sovereignty dispute and complicating Comoros' maritime jurisdiction, migration policy, and access to surrounding resources.

frictionVectors.title: External dependence in infrastructure
frictionVectors.details: Ports, energy, and connectivity projects rely heavily on foreign financing, leaving Moroni limited leverage over strategic infrastructure and maritime development.

frictionVectors.title: Cobalt and copper influence
frictionVectors.details: Foreign firms and trading networks remain deeply embedded in the copper-cobalt economy, while the state struggles to capture full value through taxation, processing, and supply-chain oversight.

frictionVectors.title: Eastern corridor insecurity
frictionVectors.details: Armed groups, regional rivalries, and contested border trade continue to undermine Kinshasa's control over mineral-rich areas and critical transport routes.

frictionVectors.title: Hydrocarbon dependence
frictionVectors.details: International oil companies remain central to production and technical capacity, limiting diversification and exposing fiscal sovereignty to external market conditions.

frictionVectors.title: Debt-backed infrastructure
frictionVectors.details: Chinese-financed roads, ports, and other projects strengthen connectivity but increase concerns over debt exposure, contract transparency, and long-term control of strategic assets.

highlights: Abidjan emerges as a regional hub

frictionVectors.title: Foreign participation in cocoa
frictionVectors.details: Global traders and processors retain substantial influence over cocoa marketing and finance, although state reforms are gradually improving producer oversight and domestic value addition.

frictionVectors.title: Port and logistics competition
frictionVectors.details: Foreign capital is important to Abidjan's port and transport expansion, creating benefits for growth while raising questions about strategic dependence and concession terms.

frictionVectors.title: Foreign military footprint
frictionVectors.details: The presence of major foreign military facilities provides revenue and security guarantees but constrains independent strategic maneuver and intensifies competition among external powers.

frictionVectors.title: Port and debt dependence
frictionVectors.details: Djibouti's logistics economy is closely tied to foreign-operated or foreign-financed port infrastructure, particularly routes serving Ethiopia, increasing exposure to debt and geopolitical pressure.

highlights: Gulf and IMF financing deepen influence

frictionVectors.title: Debt-linked asset exposure
frictionVectors.details: Heavy external financing needs increase Gulf and multilateral leverage over state assets, infrastructure priorities, and currency policy.

frictionVectors.title: Nile water insecurity
frictionVectors.details: The GERD dispute with Ethiopia continues to threaten Egypt's core water security, while regional instability complicates Red Sea and Suez revenues.

frictionVectors.title: Foreign energy dependence
frictionVectors.details: Declining mature fields and reliance on foreign operators, technology, and capital limit Equatorial Guinea's control over future production.

frictionVectors.title: Chinese infrastructure leverage
frictionVectors.details: Chinese financing and construction remain important for transport and public works, creating long-term external influence despite strong formal state control.

highlights: Mining remains the main external gateway

frictionVectors.title: Mining-sector dependency
frictionVectors.details: Foreign mining partners and commodity markets remain central to revenue generation, exposing national resource policy to external capital and price volatility.

frictionVectors.title: Red Sea strategic pressure
frictionVectors.details: Eritrea's coastline and proximity to the conflict around the Red Sea attract competing regional security interests while sanctions and diplomatic isolation constrain options.

frictionVectors.title: Customs and trade dependence
frictionVectors.details: Eswatini relies heavily on South African markets, transport networks, and the Southern African Customs Union, limiting autonomous control over trade policy.

frictionVectors.title: Sugar and industrial concentration
frictionVectors.details: Sugar, forestry, and light manufacturing remain vulnerable to external buyers, preferential trade arrangements, and infrastructure disruptions across South African corridors.

frictionVectors.title: Nile basin confrontation
frictionVectors.details: The GERD enhances Ethiopia's energy and bargaining position, but unresolved tensions with Egypt and Sudan keep water infrastructure at the center of regional rivalry.

frictionVectors.title: External financing conditionality
frictionVectors.details: Debt distress and dependence on international financial support limit policy space, while Gulf, Chinese, and Western actors compete for influence over infrastructure and logistics.

frictionVectors.title: Mining-sector renegotiation
frictionVectors.details: The transitional authorities are seeking greater state participation and local value addition in manganese and other mining projects. This creates friction with established foreign operators and investors concerned about contract stability.

frictionVectors.title: Oil dependence and infrastructure
frictionVectors.details: Gabon remains dependent on foreign technical and capital partners for offshore oil production and export logistics. Declining mature fields and limited domestic refining capacity constrain effective resource sovereignty.

frictionVectors.title: Senegambia transport asymmetry
frictionVectors.details: The Gambia relies heavily on Senegal-linked road, port, and electricity networks, improving connectivity while limiting strategic autonomy. Cross-border trade and transit arrangements remain politically sensitive.

frictionVectors.title: Foreign fishing access
frictionVectors.details: Industrial fishing access and weak monitoring continue to raise concerns over depletion of Gambian waters and lost public revenue. Enforcement capacity remains limited relative to foreign fleets and licensing interests.

frictionVectors.title: IMF and creditor conditionality
frictionVectors.details: Fiscal restructuring has increased dependence on external creditors and limits policy space for infrastructure and industrial subsidies. The government is balancing debt repair against demands for stronger domestic control of gold, oil, and emerging mineral value chains.

frictionVectors.title: Illegal mining and lithium governance
frictionVectors.details: Illegal gold mining is damaging water systems and undermining state authority, while lithium development raises pressure for transparent licensing and domestic processing. Foreign investment remains important but is being subjected to more demanding local-content expectations.

frictionVectors.title: Simandou corridor competition
frictionVectors.details: The Simandou iron-ore project is drawing major foreign capital and diplomatic attention while requiring rail and port infrastructure on an exceptional scale. The state is seeking greater revenue and downstream benefits, but contract transparency and implementation remain contentious.

frictionVectors.title: Junta-controlled mining governance
frictionVectors.details: Military rule has expanded executive control over mining licensing and infrastructure decisions without equivalent improvements in institutional oversight. Guinea retains bargaining power through bauxite and iron ore, but much of the value chain remains externally financed and operated.

frictionVectors.title: Cashew trade dependency
frictionVectors.details: The economy remains highly dependent on raw cashew exports and foreign traders, leaving producers vulnerable to price shocks and external market concentration. Limited processing capacity prevents the state from capturing a larger share of value.

frictionVectors.title: Bissau port and maritime security
frictionVectors.details: Weak port infrastructure and limited maritime enforcement create openings for opaque commercial networks and illicit trafficking. External partners can provide essential logistics and security support, but this also reduces national control over strategic gateways.

highlights: Ports and Power in Strategic Competition

frictionVectors.title: External Debt and Infrastructure Leverage
frictionVectors.details: Kenya is balancing Chinese infrastructure exposure, Western financial institutions, and domestic pressure over debt-service costs. Control of transport and energy assets remains formally national but is constrained by financing dependencies.

frictionVectors.title: Mombasa and Northern Corridor Competition
frictionVectors.details: Mombasa remains a pivotal regional gateway, drawing competition from Tanzanian and Djiboutian corridors. Foreign-backed logistics, rail, and port projects create sovereignty concerns when commercial concessions outpace public oversight.

frictionVectors.title: Lesotho Highlands Water Project
frictionVectors.details: Water exports to South Africa provide essential revenue but deepen structural dependence on a larger neighbor. Dam financing, construction delays, and benefit-sharing disputes remain sensitive sovereignty issues.

frictionVectors.title: Textile and Customs Vulnerability
frictionVectors.details: Lesotho's manufacturing base depends heavily on external markets, imported inputs, and regional trade preferences. Any changes in United States access or South African customs arrangements could rapidly weaken domestic economic autonomy.

frictionVectors.title: Iron Ore and Concession Governance
frictionVectors.details: Large-scale mining and prospective energy projects offer revenue but expose Liberia to foreign corporate leverage and uneven local benefits. Contract transparency, taxation, and environmental safeguards remain central to resource sovereignty.

frictionVectors.title: Monrovia Port and Transport Corridors
frictionVectors.details: Foreign investment is important to modernize ports, roads, and logistics, yet concession structures can limit state control over strategic infrastructure. Regional security and shipping disruptions add pressure to maintain reliable access.

highlights: Ports and Pipelines as Pressure Points

frictionVectors.title: Competing Control of Oil Institutions
frictionVectors.details: Libya's petroleum sector remains the core prize in competition among rival political and armed networks. Foreign operators and external patrons influence production, export terminals, and revenue distribution despite the formal role of national institutions.

frictionVectors.title: Foreign Military and Security Footprint
frictionVectors.details: Competing external security partnerships continue to shape access to bases, ports, and energy infrastructure. The resulting fragmentation limits Tripoli's ability to exercise consistent sovereignty across the country.

frictionVectors.title: Nickel, Cobalt, and Rare-Mineral Exposure
frictionVectors.details: Foreign-led mining operations provide export earnings and infrastructure but leave Madagascar exposed to commodity cycles, tax disputes, and limited domestic value addition. Strategic minerals increasingly attract competition among Asian and Western investors.

frictionVectors.title: Port, Power, and Connectivity Dependence
frictionVectors.details: Weak domestic electricity and transport networks increase reliance on external financiers and operators. Port modernization and telecommunications projects can improve resilience but may also create long-term leverage over critical infrastructure.

frictionVectors.title: External debt and conditionality
frictionVectors.details: Debt distress and dependence on IMF-backed reforms limit fiscal room and sovereign control over public investment. Currency and import pressures heighten exposure to external creditors.

frictionVectors.title: Mining concessions and infrastructure
frictionVectors.details: Uranium, rare-earth and graphite projects attract foreign capital, but weak state capacity creates risks that concession terms and transport infrastructure favor outside operators.

frictionVectors.title: Gold-sector renegotiation
frictionVectors.details: The government is seeking a larger state share from industrial mining, but disputes with foreign operators and opaque licensing could reduce investment while concentrating rents around the state and security elites.

frictionVectors.title: Russian security dependency
frictionVectors.details: Reliance on Russian military personnel and equipment provides regime protection but may trade strategic autonomy for privileged access to gold, logistics and other extractive opportunities.

frictionVectors.title: GTA gas governance
frictionVectors.details: The Greater Tortue Ahmeyim project with Senegal offers a major revenue and energy-security opportunity, but cross-border management and revenue-sharing remain politically sensitive.

frictionVectors.title: Foreign control of corridors
frictionVectors.details: Iron ore exports and emerging green-hydrogen plans depend on foreign capital, ports and rail infrastructure, leaving Mauritania exposed to investor bargaining power and project delays.

frictionVectors.title: Indian Ocean strategic competition
frictionVectors.details: The Chagos and Diego Garcia issue continues to affect Mauritius's maritime sovereignty and relations with the United Kingdom, the United States and India.

frictionVectors.title: External dependence in energy and food
frictionVectors.details: Mauritius retains strong institutional control but remains structurally dependent on imported fuel, food and strategic shipping links, leaving it vulnerable to global price and supply shocks.

highlights: Phosphate and renewable capacity reinforce leverage
Western Sahara remains the central sovereignty front

frictionVectors.title: Western Sahara resource diplomacy
frictionVectors.details: Morocco's control of the territory and its fisheries, phosphates and renewable projects remains contested by the Polisario Front and Algeria, complicating trade and diplomatic recognition.

frictionVectors.title: Water and energy infrastructure
frictionVectors.details: Drought and water stress are driving costly desalination and transfer projects, while dependence on imported energy and foreign technology creates exposure despite expanding renewables.

highlights: Cabo Delgado Remains a Sovereignty Test

frictionVectors.title: Cabo Delgado Insurgency
frictionVectors.details: Insurgent violence continues to constrain state control around gas projects and raises dependence on Rwandan and regional security forces. Foreign investors retain significant leverage over the timing and terms of LNG development.

frictionVectors.title: LNG and Port Concessions
frictionVectors.details: International energy firms and logistics operators dominate major resource corridors, limiting domestic value capture despite expected fiscal gains. Contract transparency and local-content enforcement remain politically sensitive.

frictionVectors.title: Offshore Oil Dependence
frictionVectors.details: Major offshore discoveries have intensified competition among international energy companies for exploration rights. Namibia is seeking stronger state participation and local benefits while avoiding overdependence on foreign capital and technology.

frictionVectors.title: Critical Minerals and Hydrogen Finance
frictionVectors.details: European, Chinese, and Gulf-backed investors are competing for uranium, lithium, and green-hydrogen opportunities. Infrastructure financing could accelerate development but may constrain policy autonomy if projects rely heavily on external guarantees.

frictionVectors.title: Uranium and Mining Renegotiation
frictionVectors.details: The military government is pressing foreign mining interests for greater state control and revenue, particularly in uranium. Disputes with established operators risk production disruptions and legal confrontation.

frictionVectors.title: Oil Pipeline Vulnerability
frictionVectors.details: The crude export route through Benin remains exposed to diplomatic tension, border insecurity, and regional political estrangement. Niger's withdrawal from Western-backed security structures has narrowed its logistics and financing options.

frictionVectors.title: Pipeline Theft and Militancy
frictionVectors.details: Oil theft, attacks, and sabotage continue to reduce production and weaken federal control over the Niger Delta. Security dependence on private contractors and local intermediaries complicates sovereign management of energy infrastructure.

frictionVectors.title: Foreign Capital and Infrastructure Leverage
frictionVectors.details: Chinese, Gulf, European, and other investors remain important to ports, rail, power, and energy projects. Financing needs give external partners bargaining power even as domestic refining capacity improves Nigeria's strategic room.

frictionVectors.title: Eastern Congo Mineral Networks
frictionVectors.details: Rwanda faces sustained international scrutiny over alleged support for M23 and the movement of coltan and other minerals through regional trading networks. Sanctions pressure and diplomatic isolation risks could affect its export model and security partnerships.

frictionVectors.title: Donor and Investment Dependence
frictionVectors.details: Rwanda's infrastructure and development model remains reliant on foreign aid, concessional finance, and multinational investment. This supports state capacity but leaves Kigali vulnerable to conditionality over regional conduct and governance.

frictionVectors.title: Offshore exploration uncertainty
frictionVectors.details: Prospects in the Joint Development Zone with Nigeria have not translated into dependable petroleum revenues. São Tomé remains vulnerable to outside operators setting the terms of any future development.

frictionVectors.title: External financing dependence
frictionVectors.details: The government relies heavily on concessional donors and foreign investment for infrastructure and energy security, limiting fiscal room for fully autonomous policy.

frictionVectors.title: Sangomar and GTA contract scrutiny
frictionVectors.details: Senegal is seeking greater transparency and domestic value from offshore projects operated with international partners. Revenue expectations are high, while production, contract terms, and fiscal constraints create political sensitivity.

frictionVectors.title: Debt and infrastructure exposure
frictionVectors.details: Large infrastructure and energy projects depend on foreign capital, contractors, and lenders. Debt-service pressures may narrow Dakar's ability to renegotiate projects or prioritize local industrial participation.

frictionVectors.title: External control of maritime infrastructure
frictionVectors.details: Seychelles depends on foreign partners for port modernization, maritime surveillance, and connectivity across its vast exclusive economic zone. Competition among India, China, Gulf states, and Western partners requires careful sovereignty management.

frictionVectors.title: Climate and debt vulnerability
frictionVectors.details: Sea-level rise, coastal damage, and dependence on tourism expose the state to external finance and insurance conditions. Blue-bond and conservation-finance arrangements can support resilience but may constrain policy flexibility.

frictionVectors.title: Iron ore and rutile dependency
frictionVectors.details: Foreign-led mining operations dominate export earnings and infrastructure investment, leaving fiscal performance exposed to commodity prices and operational disputes. The state continues to face pressure to secure better royalties, processing, and community benefits.

frictionVectors.title: Debt-financed infrastructure
frictionVectors.details: Road, port, and energy projects rely substantially on external lenders and contractors, including Chinese and other international firms. Repayment obligations and opaque commercial terms can reduce long-term control over strategic assets.

frictionVectors.title: Foreign competition over ports
frictionVectors.details: Turkey, the United Arab Emirates, Qatar, and other partners compete for influence over ports, logistics, security, and maritime access. Federal-state disputes over authority make it difficult for Somalia to negotiate from a unified sovereign position.

frictionVectors.title: Al-Shabaab and offshore-resource risk
frictionVectors.details: Insurgent violence constrains state control of territory, transport corridors, and potential resource zones. Offshore hydrocarbons and fisheries remain vulnerable to contested licensing, illegal exploitation, and security-dependent foreign operators.

highlights: Grid and rail bottlenecks constrain sovereignty

frictionVectors.title: Mineral-processing dependence
frictionVectors.details: South Africa retains substantial mineral reserves but remains exposed to foreign capital, commodity-price cycles, and external demand for platinum-group metals, manganese, and other strategic minerals. Efforts to expand domestic processing compete with infrastructure and electricity constraints.

frictionVectors.title: Logistics infrastructure stress
frictionVectors.details: Port congestion, rail underperformance, and unreliable electricity weaken state control over export corridors and raise dependence on private operators and external financiers. Regional competition for mineral routes adds pressure on national infrastructure planning.

frictionVectors.title: Oil transit vulnerability
frictionVectors.details: South Sudan's fiscal survival depends on oil exported through Sudanese infrastructure, leaving revenue and sovereignty vulnerable to conflict, pipeline disruption, and bargaining by neighboring authorities. Chinese and regional commercial interests remain important to the sector.

frictionVectors.title: Fragmented security patronage
frictionVectors.details: Elite competition, armed factions, and external mediation continue to shape access to territory and resources. Weak institutions limit the government's ability to regulate land, oil, and cross-border trade independently.

frictionVectors.title: Gold and armed financing
frictionVectors.details: Gold production and smuggling provide revenue to competing armed actors and attract foreign intermediaries, reducing civilian state control over a strategic export. Sanctions and opaque trading networks further complicate formal resource governance.

frictionVectors.title: Port and pipeline leverage
frictionVectors.details: Control of Port Sudan, oil infrastructure, and transport corridors has become strategically valuable amid the civil war. Regional powers and commercial actors seek influence over logistics, humanitarian access, and future reconstruction terms.

frictionVectors.title: Mining-contract pressure
frictionVectors.details: Tanzania is seeking greater domestic participation, taxation, and processing in gold and critical-mineral projects while still relying on foreign capital and expertise. Contract renegotiations and local-content demands can generate friction with international investors.

frictionVectors.title: Port and corridor competition
frictionVectors.details: Upgrades around Dar es Salaam and regional rail corridors increase Tanzania's strategic role for neighboring landlocked economies. External financing and competition with Kenyan and Mozambican routes create sovereignty risks if infrastructure dependence becomes concentrated.

frictionVectors.title: Port dependency and external capital
frictionVectors.details: The Port of Lomé strengthens Togo's role in Gulf of Guinea trade and Sahel connectivity, but operations and expansion remain dependent on foreign investment, logistics firms, and regional security conditions. This limits the state's autonomy over critical commercial infrastructure.

frictionVectors.title: Phosphate-sector governance
frictionVectors.details: Phosphates remain a major strategic asset, yet production and processing face institutional, investment, and market constraints. External financing and commodity demand strongly influence the sector's contribution to national development.

highlights: EU Leverage Over Migration and Finance

frictionVectors.title: EU Migration Bargaining
frictionVectors.details: European financial and political support remains tied to migration containment, giving Brussels significant leverage over Tunisia's domestic and external choices.

frictionVectors.title: Gas and Electricity Exposure
frictionVectors.details: Tunisia relies heavily on imported energy and Algerian gas, while fiscal constraints slow investment in domestic production and renewables.

frictionVectors.title: EACOP Financing and Environmental Disputes
frictionVectors.details: The Uganda-Tanzania oil pipeline remains central to export strategy but faces sustained opposition over land acquisition, environmental risks, and external financing constraints.

frictionVectors.title: Strategic Infrastructure Dependence
frictionVectors.details: Chinese contractors and Gulf investors are increasingly important to transport, energy, and extractive projects, raising concerns over debt exposure and long-term revenue control.

frictionVectors.title: Foreign Control of Copper Value Chains
frictionVectors.details: New investment from Gulf, Chinese, and Western-linked firms is expanding copper capacity, but Zambia continues to struggle to secure greater domestic refining, taxation, and processing benefits.

frictionVectors.title: Power Shortages Threaten Industrial Strategy
frictionVectors.details: Hydropower deficits and drought-related generation shocks constrain mining and manufacturing, increasing reliance on imported electricity and private-sector infrastructure.

frictionVectors.title: Lithium and Platinum Concession Pressure
frictionVectors.details: Chinese and other foreign investors dominate major critical-mineral projects, while Zimbabwe's beneficiation ambitions remain limited by capital shortages, sanctions, and weak regulatory credibility.

frictionVectors.title: Infrastructure-for-Resources Exposure
frictionVectors.details: The government increasingly uses mineral concessions and production agreements to secure energy, transport, and mining infrastructure, risking opaque terms and reduced sovereign capture of future revenues.
